combined_title: Jada Langston Dissertation Defense: Lake Erie Hydrology Over the last 15 ka: Insights from Stable isotope Geochemistry, Water Balance Modeling and Bulk Geochemistry
event_subtitle: Lake Erie Hydrology Over the last 15 ka: Insights from Stable isotope Geochemistry, Water Balance Modeling and Bulk Geochemistry
description:
Sedimentary archives in lakes have been crucial for reconstructing climatic and hydrologic conditions of Earth’s past. The oxygen isotope records from skeletal materials are a key part of the toolkit for studying past climate with extensive use in marine and terrestrial settings including in lakes. For the Laurentide Great Lakes in North America, δ18O values (δ18Ocarb) of molluscs and ostracods (biogenic carbonates) have helped us understand their formation following the melting of the Laurentide Ice Sheet, subsequent isostatic rebound, and regional climate change over the past 15 ka. Biogenic carbonate δ18Ocarb values from Lake Erie, the shallowest of the Laurentide Great Lakes, have been critical for understanding its water balance, which is very sensitive to hydroclimate fluctuations. This works because δ18Ocarb values reflect the isotopic composition of lake water (δ18Olw), which is very sensitive to changes in lake evaporation or input sources. However, δ18Ocarb is a function of multiple hydrologic (temperature, humidity, evaporation, input sources) and isotopic levers (the isotopic composition of lake and atmosphere) which can significantly impact the δ18Ocarb value. In this dissertation, I demonstrate the advantages of evaluating the δ18Ocarb data in relation to regional water balance, lake configuration, and temperature constraints over the last 15 ka. 

Chapter 2 characterizes the modern hydrological conditions of Lake Erie by evaluating the seasonal and temporal isotopic (δ18Olw, δ2Hlw, and δ’17Olw) variability of local precipitation, river, and lake water within the lake basin. Our results show a systematic variation in δ18Olwr, d-excess and Δ17Owater data of lake waters in relation to seasonal conditions and basin location. I then utilize the well-monitored hydrological system of the Great Lakes to constrain the fraction of moisture from the lake (f) parameter and the ratio of turbulent to diffusive fractionation (phi or n) parameter for Lake Erie. Both parameters are essential to the lake-water isotope mass balance models and significantly affect the isotopic composition of the water (δ18Owater) but are poorly constrained. I show initial studies constraints on f and phi are too restricted and I proposed an updated look at the variation in f and phi values.

Chapter 3 employs the isotope mass balance framework established in Chapter 2 for paleohydrology reconstructions of Lake Erie. I utilize biogenic carbonates from sediment cores from the eastern and western basin of Lake Erie to reconstruct the isotopic composition of formation water (δ18Ofw) in respect to changing lake configurations and temperatures over the last 15ka. This chapter reviews previous assumptions about lake hydrology in relation to input sources, lake evaporation, and basin dynamics and suggests that a water balance modeling approach can be used as an additional measure to constrain lake conditions. I demonstrate with mass balance modeling that Lake Erie was an evaporative lake during from ~15 to 10 ka, contrary to previous interpretations that Lake Erie was a high stand lake. After 10 ka, our mass balance approach supports previous interpretations suggesting that Lake Erie transitioned to a highly evaporative closed basin lake before shifting to its modern hydrology ~5ka. 

Chapter 4 seeks to utilize micrite samples from the same sediment cores in Chapter 3 to evaluate whether lake micrite can reconstruct regional paleoclimate. Using x-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and clumped isotope geochemistry (Δ47), I analyzed samples for detrital contamination and whether these samples can be used to contextualize regional landscape changes in the Lake Erie basin. I find that all samples from the eastern and central basin have detrital contamination with reconstructed Δ47 temperatures ranging between 45 to 64°C. No micrite Δ47 temperature matches modern lake temperatures but matches previous Paleozoic and Mesozoic detrital limestone clasts Δ47 temperatures. 

This dissertation represents a more extensive application of water balance modeling for paleoclimate applications and contributes abundant isotopic (δ18Olw, δ2Hlw, δ’17Olw, δ18Ocarb, δ13Ccarb, and Δ47) data for modern and paleo-lake systems. The data from this dissertation illuminates a strong connection between the water balance of Lake Erie, lake evaporation, and the Laurentide ice sheet both in the modern lake and paleohydrology.

description: Engendering Respectful Communities (ERC) is a one session workshop that engages graduate students in meaningful dialogue about various forms of sexual misconduct they may encounter in both professional and social spaces, and provides resources for intervention or support in such circumstances.The primary goal of the workshop is to address complexities experienced by graduate students as they engage in bystander intervention, so that participants gain an increase in awareness of barriers to action and familiarity with strategic planning to overcome them. The workshop also introduces participants to on-campus resources and provides knowledge on how sexual misconduct can unfold in graduate-specific settings.The ERC workshop uses small-group circles intended to promote active reflection and space to build community. The procedure of circles is introduced at the beginning of the workshop in order to help participants get used to the process, which they do through a circle for introductions and value-sharing for the workshop space. These circles depict various, realistic scenarios related to sexual misconduct within the graduate community. The circle process allows circle members to process the monologues, reflect on complexities with identity and power dynamics within them, name potential barriers to intervention, and think of various ways in which they might respond if faced with similar situations. The circles provide a way to foster collective building of ideas, where participants learn from one another and all input is equally valued. Participants are encouraged to share but can always pass if desired, creating an environment where participation is open but not forced. Due to the participatory nature of the workshop, if you are to arrive more than 20 minutes late, we will ask you to re-register for another workshop session.If you have any questions about or concerns with taking this workshop, or are in need of an exemption, please contact jhippe@umich.edu or fill out this form. We know some students come to campus having already experienced harm. If you have circumstances that make completing this course challenging, please reach out to the GROWE team. SAPAC GROWE provides exemptions to the ERC workshop (where requirements are set in place) on a case by case basis. event_title: The Greek Manuscripts of the University of Michigan: A Celebration of the Collection and Its Catalogue
combined_title: The Greek Manuscripts of the University of Michigan: A Celebration of the Collection and Its Catalogue
description:
Join us to celebrate the culmination of a decade-and-a-half-long project to fully catalog the University of Michigan Library’s extraordinary collection of Greek manuscripts. 

A Catalogue of Greek Manuscripts, Volume 2 (https://myumi.ch/NXVQr), published by U-M Press, brings this monumental undertaking to a close, making one of the most extensive collections of Greek manuscripts in North America accessible to scholars around the world.

Enjoy breakfast refreshments while three scholars offer complementary perspectives on the study of Greek manuscripts:

THE MAKING OF A CATALOGUE OF GREEK MANUSCRIPTS AT THE UNIVERSITY OF MICHIGAN: CHALLENGES, ACHIEVEMENT, AND DISCOVERIES with Nadezhda Kavrus-Hoffmann, cataloger of U-M’s Greek manuscript collection.

Volume 2 covers eighty-four manuscripts and fragments. Overall, these manuscripts span a thousand years of history, from the ninth to the nineteenth century, and include a wide range of subjects, from Bible texts and saints' lives to church music and secular writing.

Learn about the detective work behind the project, including three especially exciting finds: a small fragment that turned out to preserve lost portions of a medieval Byzantine text on Indian mathematics; a beautifully illuminated fourteenth-century manuscript paired with poetry written specifically for it; and a manuscript that may be traced back to the personal library of a nineteenth-century monk-scholar, opening a new mystery about how it came to Michigan.

THE PRINCESS AND THE PHILOSOPHER: ANNA COMNENA AND THE MANUSCRIPTS OF ARISTOTLE'S "ETHICS" with Richard Janko, professor of Greek in the Department of Classical Studies, who has drawn on the collection for teaching and research.

The Byzantine historian and would-be empress Anna Comnena, confined for life to a nunnery in Constantinople after trying to depose her imperial brother, was a passionate philosopher. Beginning in 1118 C.E. she organized a scholarly edition of Aristotle's "Nicomachean Ethics" and induced three other scholars to write commentaries on it. Several remarkable paper manuscripts, now precisely datable because they belong to her project, reflect this effort. They show how her team evolved useful conventions like the comma and the footnote-number, and worked with Italian scholars to create the earliest translation of this work into Latin. 

ALWAYS INTERESTING: SELECTED BINDINGS FROM THE UM GREEK MANUSCRIPT COLLECTION with Julia Miller, bookbinding historian and contributor to the catalogue.

Miller will focus on a selection of bindings, looking at their structure, materials, and decoration — chosen based on gorgeous images in the catalogue of bindings ranging from small and exquisite, Mich. Ms. 68 (15th century), and larger but equally beautiful, Mich. Ms. 172 (14th century), both in their original and completely traditional Greek bindings, to the fascinating layers of repair and rebinding represented by Mich. Ms. 76 (17th century).

event_title: Collaborative Intelligence: Learning Together from Heterogeneous Data and Language
combined_title: Collaborative Intelligence: Learning Together from Heterogeneous Data and Language: Raed Al Kontar
description: Data are increasingly generated by many connected users, machines, and systems, which has led to explosive interest in collaborative analytics, such as federated learning, that borrow strength across diverse sources. To date, these efforts have focused mainly on predictive modeling. In this talk, I argue that collaboration, without untangling the nature of heterogeneity across users, can lead to swift and evident failures. Indeed, borrowing from the wrong sources can be worse than not collaborating at all. To this end, I present two frameworks that address two questions at the heart of collaboration: what to share, and whom to borrow from. First, we introduce Personalized PCA, a descriptive framework that extracts interpretable and identifiable features describing what is shared and what is unique across diverse datasets. Second, I bring language into the collaboration. When a new user has too little data to tell which collaborators are relevant, expert textual descriptions of the new system, often available yet overlooked, can fill the gap. Here, a large language model translates these descriptions into a prior over source relevance that guides learning when data are scarce and is gradually corrected as data accumulate. I conclude by highlighting future directions at the intersection of agentic AI, statistics, and decision making.

Seats are offered on a first come, first served basis; please arrive early to secure a spot. Login here (no pre-registration needed): https://myumi.ch/ZellWriters26

Tisa Bryant’s writing explores Black women’s subjectivity by remixing rhetorical, literary, cinematic and visual arts techniques into original modes of narrative and storytelling.  Her latest book, *Residual*, is an assemblage of the interiors of grief, the home as archive, and the mystery of mothers, published by Nightboat Books in 2026. Her first book, *Unexplained Presence*, on the mythologies of Black presences in the arts, was reissued by Wave Books in 2024. In her afterword to *Unexplained Presence*, renowned critic Margo Jefferson hailed Tisa as a “literary and film auteur, an auteur of performance on the page, stage and screen or canvas.” 

A Boston native, Tisa was a member of the Dark Room Collective, an African-diasporic writing group that hosted a celebrated reading series in Cambridge and Boston.  She is co-editor of the three-volume, cross-referenced literary journal, *The Encyclopedia Project*, and collaborated from 2015-2018 with critic and writer Ernest Hardy on *The Black Book*, an original talk and film series presented at the Hammer Museum in Los Angeles. Tisa is editor of *Deep West Assembly*, a monograph of recent works by the award-winning visual artist Cauleen Smith, forthcoming in 2026 from Astrup Fearnley Museet and Kestner Gesellschaft. She lives in Iowa City, where she is Associate Professor of English in the Nonfiction Writing Program at the University of Iowa, and is currently at work on a novel.

event_title: Double Duty: A Subsidy Design for\\Quality Promotion and Price Discipline
combined_title: Double Duty: A Subsidy Design for\\Quality Promotion and Price Discipline: Ying Fan, University of Michigan
description: This paper studies how the design of quality-linked subsidies shapes firm behavior in both quality choices and pricing decisions. We examine a major reform in Medicare Advantage that links subsidies to quality through two distinct policy parameters. We develop and estimate a structural model of demand and firm behavior to evaluate the reform, decompose its effects, and compare alternative quality-linked subsidy designs. A central finding is that a subsidy design that links product quality to both the subsidy level and the pass-through from firm prices to subsidized consumer prices can simultaneously raise quality and lower prices.

event_title: Accessible Field Paleontology: Building Community through Universal Design in the Field
combined_title: Accessible Field Paleontology: Building Community through Universal Design in the Field: Tara Lepore
description:
Accessible Field Paleontology: Building Community through Universal Design in the Field
Taormina (Tara) Lepore, Ph.D.
Assistant Professor
Mallinson Institute for Science Education
Department of Geological and Environmental Sciences
Western Michigan University
Friday, Oct. 23, 2026 - University of Michigan Paleontology Seminar

Field paleontology is a standout experience in the training and education of many paleontologists. It is to our benefit to build accessible, welcoming field paleontology experiences so all may learn and thrive in the field. Disabled people in particular face barriers to full, equitable field participation, but efforts have been made to create and assess disability accessible field experiences in geology and other field sciences. Field paleontology is one area where the science education and accessibility literature as well as practical availability of accessible field work is less widely reported. In this talk, I encourage our community to ask: What can we do, as paleontologists, to be at the forefront of accessible and equitable field experiences for all?

As a paleontologist and a discipline-based geoscience education researcher, I will discuss my path in science and the rationale for this type of work. A brief overview of the relevant accessible science education and outreach literature on accessible field work will be discussed, as well as current research efforts to build affirming classroom and field environments that utilize Universal Design and the theoretical frameworks of humanizing STEM and culturally relevant pedagogy, all with a disability focus. Finally, this talk will highlight a recent accessible field paleontology experience in the metro Denver area at the annual meeting of the Geological Society of America, where field participants engaged in both the local paleontology and in accessible pedagogy, and the access needs of all participants were considered at the forefront. Universal Design and the related theoretical frameworks can help us consider everyone who is present in a field paleontology experience, and can truly lead to a more accessible, inclusive, and thriving paleontological community at large.

description:
From September 2025 through December 2026, Stamps Gallery is partnering in a curatorial collaboration with two Southeast Michigan-based, artist-run project spaces led by Stamps alumni: C.Y.N.K. Studios, directed by Sally Clegg (Lecturer III and Student Exhibition Coordinator, MFA ’20) and Abhishek Narula (MFA ’20); and Sometimes Space, directed by Nathan Byrne (Lecturer I, MFA ’21). Artist Statements/Bios

Abhishek Narula, Compressions 
Compressions is an installation comprised of 416 industrial-grade zip ties, cinched around the entry pillar of the Stamps Gallery. The pillar measures roughly 110 inches in circumference, requiring two ties per row to wrap around it, resulting in 208 rows. The humble zip tie, typically used to hang and bind other material, is relegated to its functional properties rendering it unprepossessing and easily dismissed. The zip tie in this installation, instead serves as an object of aesthetic possibility, pulling it out of its usual background role to become the work itself. The resulting composition is a proposal to dwell, to slow down, and to simply see the pillar.

Abhishek Narula is an artist, designer, and educator who works across sculpture, installation, sound, and video. His practice takes the form of interventions, working with what is already present. He reorients and disrupts objects and sites in order to open up formal possibilities and poetic experiences within the familiar. He is influenced by physical and digital infrastructural systems that sustain modern life and culture. His work treats this ambience itself as raw material for aesthetic inquiry, exploring themes of labor, precarity, temporality and the sublime. Narula earned his MFA in Studio Art from the University of Michigan Stamps School of Art & Design and his MS/BS in Electrical Engineering from the Georgia Institute of Technology. His work has been exhibited at national and international venues such as the Ammerman Center for Arts and Technology, Science Gallery Detroit, Speculum Artium Media Festival in Slovenia, New Media Caucus (NMC), WaveFarm, The Boulder Public Library, The Hyde Park Art Center, Sector 2337 Art Gallery & Printing Press, Tangible Embedded Interaction (TEI), International Symposium of Electronic Arts (ISEA), among others. He is a Robotics Systems Designer and Lecturer in the Robotics Department at the University of Michigan. Website / Instagram

Nathan Byrne, Equally To Be Loved
Equally To Be Loved is an image / object scaled to and installed upon the courtyard pillar of Stamps Gallery. The image is of a spontaneous sculpture made in 2017 during the first day of an artist residency at the Recology San Francisco A.I.R. Program. The sculpture was constructed in a storage container studio using 14 discrete objects that were in his studio upon entry. For Byrne, this work embodies the energy and spirit of a studio at the start of a particularly fecund period of making. This work speaks to the artist’s interest in embodied experience of space, archival and site responsiveness, as well as his ongoing engagement with found materials. Byrne considers this project to be a far-flung sequel to his MFA thesis exhibition Equally Empty, which was shown at Stamps Gallery in 2021. Equally To Be Loved is the second line of the Buddhist mantra from which both titles are derived.

Nathan Byrne is an artist / educator / curator currently based in Detroit, MI. Through spatial and archive responsive projects, he reimagines, and explores within frameworks such as language, the passage of time, and contemplation. Intrigued by the potential of conveying phenomenal, transformative, and emotive states through materiality, process, and placement, he negotiates the pliability of the viewer’s encounters with objects and environments. Byrne holds an MFA in Art from the University of Michigan Stamps School of Art & Design and a BA in Studio Art and Art History from San Francisco State University. He has been a Lecturer at Stamps School of Art & Design since the Fall of 2022. His work is exhibited widely nationally and he is a recipient of the VSC Fellowship at Vermont Studio Center. He has been awarded numerous artist residencies including Anderson Ranch Arts Center, I-Park, KHN Center for the Arts, Prairie Ronde, Recology San Francisco A.I.R. Program, and Rockland Woods. description:
A reverie is a state between waking and dreaming, a moment when the mind drifts beyond the immediate. It is a space where memory, imagination, desire, and reality can overlap, distort, and take on new forms. In these moments, the familiar can become strange, and the ordinary can become something unexpected.

Reverie brings together student works that explore the space between what is known and what is felt. Across painting, oil pastel, ceramic, digital art, animation, and mixed media, the artists move through imagined landscapes, intimate encounters, memories, figures, and fragments of the everyday. These works blur the boundaries between observation and imagination, allowing emotion and perception to reshape what we recognize.

Rather than depicting dreams literally, Reverie considers dreaming as a way of seeing. The works reflect moments of escape, introspection, fantasy, and transformation, where the subconscious can surface and reality becomes open to interpretation. 

Reverie was conceived and curated by members of the Student-led Exhibition Committee (SEC), and features work by eight SEC members at the Stamps School of Art & Design. The exhibition includes ten works across oil on canvas, oil pastel, ceramic, digital art, digital animation, and mixed media.

combined_title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
description:
Changes over the course of the nineteenth century in how Americans voted, from voice vote to public ballot box to private voting booth, also saw changes in the material culture that surrounded voting. Ballots and ballot boxes, campaign pins and ribbons, blank lists and pre-printed party tickets, lanterns and banners–the creative forces of the American print industry filled the country’s cities and small towns with the ephemera of electioneering.

As you look at the items in this exhibit, think about what they tell us about how Americans in the past felt about voting, and about how voting felt. How did Election Days feel when they were full of parades and music and public drinking? What was it like to vote when everyone around you knew who you voted for? And, most of all, who counted as a voter, and who did the counting?

On view September 11-December 22, weekdays from 12-4 pm.

description:
Curated by Srimoyee Mitra

Stamps Gallery kicks off the fall 2026 semester with an ambitious mid-career survey of interdisciplinary artist Cosmo Whyte. Born and raised in Jamaica, Whyte completed a BFA from Bennington College and earned an MFA from the University of Michigan. He is currently a faculty member at the School of the Arts and Architecture, UCLA.

This exhibition brings together two central concerns that animate Whyte’s artistic practice: the archive, both personal and public, as a site of disturbance; and migration as a lived experience of refuge, refusal, and reinvention. In Whyte’s work, the archive is never static or neutral. Rather, it is a contested space where official histories encounter memory, inheritance, and the fragments of stories carried across generations. His practice moves within this charged interstitial terrain, between what has been recorded and what has been remembered, between institutional knowledge and embodied experience. Whyte invites the viewer to consider the fluidity of geographic borders and layered cultural identities that have persisted despite societal unrest caused by racial and socio-economic hierarchies across generations. In an era of intensified border politics and renewed debates over national identity, Whyte’s work offers a timely meditation on memory, movement, and belonging.

Presented with support from the U-M Institute for Humanities, the U-M LSA Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies, and the U-M Library.

combined_title: The Human Odyssey on the Roof of the World: Adaptations and Resilience on the Tibetan Plateau: Dr. Yuchao Zhao, Assistant Curator of East Asian Anthropology,  Field Museum of Natural History, Chicago
event_subtitle: Dr. Yuchao Zhao, Assistant Curator of East Asian Anthropology,  Field Museum of Natural History, Chicago
description: The Tibetan Plateau—often described as the “Roof of the World”—represents one of the most extreme environments ever inhabited by humans. With an average elevation exceeding 4000 meters, the region poses formidable challenges including hypoxia, harsh climate, and highly variable ecological productivity. Understanding how and when humans successfully adapted to these conditions remains a central question in high-altitude archaeology. This talk synthesizes recent archaeological, paleoenvironmental, and genetic research to reassess the long-term history of human occupation on the Tibetan Plateau. Evidence from Paleolithic sites indicates that foraging populations began exploring the plateau margins as early as the Middle Pleistocene, with increasing evidence for sustained human presence during the Late Pleistocene and early Holocene. Rather than viewing the plateau as permanently settled only after the arrival of agriculture and pastoralism, new research suggests that indigenous foragers played a crucial role in establishing viable lifeways in high-altitude environments.

combined_title: 3rd Spaceout International Ambisonics Festival
description:
A spatial audio festival presented by the Department of Performing Arts Technology.

Join us to celebrate and experience ambisonics, an immersive audio technology that surrounds you with sound from all directions. This year’s festival will feature fixed-media works, live performances and interactive works and virtual reality (VR) experiences designed with Inviso.

All events are free and open to the public. Seating is limited and available on a first-come, first-served basis.

PROGRAM
Concert 1: October 22 at 7:00 pm
Concert 2: October 23 at 12:30 pm
Concert 3: October 23 at 4:30 pm
Inviso session: October 23, 12:00–6:00 pm @ the Edit Rooms and Music Technology Library (MTL)

combined_title: Walk to the Polls: SEAS Walk to the Polls 2027
description: Join SEAS and Turn Up Turnout for a Walk to the Polls event. We’ll gather in the Ford Commons on the first floor of the Dana Building for food and then walk together to the U-M Museum of Art (UMMA), one of U-M’s on-campus voting hubs. Eligible voters can cast their ballot at UMMA, while others are welcome to join us to learn more about the voting process.This is a nonpartisan event. All members of the SEAS and PitE community are welcome!

description:

Along the way, you’ll also find a community of peers, alumni, and U-M staff who are here to support you and cheer you on.

combined_title: Guided Tour of the Clements Library
description: Join us this Parent and Family Weekend for a guided tour to learn more about the Clements’ early American history collections. Highlights include viewing of Benjamin West’s iconic painting “Death of General Wolfe,” a Revolutionary War-era trunk that once housed General Gage’s papers, and viewing our current exhibit Who Counts? A History of Voting in America! To register or get more information about this event, please contact the Development team at clemdevcom@umich.edu.
